lines: Imagine falling from the sky through a violent storm and waking up alone in a deadly jungle.
On 24 December 1971 a passenger plane is struck by lightning and breaks apart midair.
Seventeen year old Juliane Koepcke falls about 3000 meters while still strapped to her seat row.
She wakes up on the dark forest floor with a broken collarbone and a deep arm cut.
She also suffers from a painful eye injury and a severe concussion after the terrifying plunge.
Her biologist father previously taught her that following flowing water always leads back to people.
She finds a tiny creek and begins walking through the dense and dangerous Peruvian rainforest.
Days pass slowly as she follows the winding water toward a larger and safer river.
Up to 14 other passengers survive the initial crash but tragically die before any rescue arrives.
She spends 11 long days completely alone in the unforgiving jungle facing unimaginable odds.
After 9 days of difficult travel she finally discovers a remote lumberjack camp by the river.
She is found by local workers who provide medical help and bring her back to safety.
Juliane remains the only official survivor of LANSA Flight 508 against all odds and expectations.
Would you have the mental strength to survive 11 days alone in the dangerous rainforest?

lines: If you fall through lake ice, do not start swimming toward the nearest dry bank.
Mark steps onto the frozen lake, unaware he has only 10 minutes to save himself.
Suddenly, a loud crack echoes, and the freezing water swallows Mark under the dark ice.
Cold shock strikes immediately, leaving him just 1 minute to control his heavy, gasping breathing.
He remembers the 1-10-1 rule before cold water robs his body of all muscle control.
One. Turn back around toward the exact direction you just walked from right away.
That specific path of ice already proved it can hold your full body weight safely.
Two. Place your arms flat on the solid ice surface and kick your legs hard.
Get your body completely horizontal in the water, then pull your chest up onto ice.
Three. Do not stand up once your body climbs out onto the slippery surface.
Instead, Mark crouches low and rolls away from the hole to spread his body weight.
Rolling across the thin ice prevents a second break while keeping him out of water.
Mark begins crawling carefully toward the tree-lined shore to reach safety and warm shelter.
He follows every safety step correctly to escape the freezing lake in record time.
It was the perfect escape plan, but there was just one major problem remaining.
Wet clothes freeze instantly in subzero air, giving him 1 hour before hypothermia strikes.
part1.cliffhanger: Mark pulled himself out of the freezing water, but his wet clothes are freezing solid in subzero air.
